summary: This work demonstrates an inverse-design workflow for superconducting transmon qubits that maps target Hamiltonian parameters ($f_q$ and $\alpha$) directly to component-level layout parameters via a neural network paired with a frozen forward surrogate. Validation against conventional EM simulation achieves mean percent errors of 0.73% for qubit frequency and 1.58% for anharmonicity on 97 geometrically usable designs, with speedups of $3.9 \times 10^7$ on CPU and $4.6 \times 10^7$ on GPU at batch size 2048 relative to single EM extractions.
motivation: Designing superconducting qubits currently requires iterative forward-loop simulation with expensive EM solvers, creating a bottleneck in QPU design. Direct mapping from target Hamiltonian parameters to physical geometry would accelerate candidate generation and enable systematic exploration of design space.
method: An inverse MLP with one hidden layer (64 units, 387 parameters) was trained using a frozen forward-surrogate MLP (736 units, 4418 parameters) to enforce loss in Hamiltonian space rather than geometry space, addressing the ill-posed one-to-many nature of the inverse problem. Training used $\sim$1,000 samples from the SQuADDS cross-claw transmon dataset with min-max scaling and mean absolute error loss on scaled Hamiltonian parameters.
result: On 97 valid EM-validated designs from held-out SQuADDS test records, the pipeline achieves median errors of 0.53% ($f_q$) and 1.14% ($\alpha$), comparable to combined simulation-to-measurement uncertainty for academic transmon processes. Single-sample inference takes $\sim$60 ms on CPU versus $\sim$2 min for conventional EM extraction; batched inference reaches 3.1 µs per sample on CPU and 2.6 µs on GPU, enabling rapid screening of candidate designs.
